title: King takes up ahimsa
hookLine: a Baptist pastor credits a Hindu lawyer with his method. how?
carry: ahimsa: non-harm that wins the opponent over
tomorrow: why would King call his trip to India a pilgrimage?
last: THE FRUIT WAS NEVER YOURS TO HOLD.

lines: CHRIST THE SPIRIT, GANDHI THE METHOD.
cards: Plenty of people pick up something that lasts from someone of another faith: a coach, a neighbor, a teacher at the gym.
Martin Luther King Jr. did it in front of the whole country, and he left behind an odd sentence about it. A Baptist pastor, writing about the movement he led, gives the credit to two people.
Christ, he says, gave the spirit and the motivation. Gandhi, a Hindu lawyer from the other side of the world, gave the method. So how does a Baptist pastor end up with a Hindu's method?

teach.b: In Stride Toward Freedom, his book about the Montgomery bus boycott, King says that as a seminary student in Pennsylvania he had nearly decided that love works between two people and fails against a whole unjust system.

teach.h: A SERMON, THEN A STACK OF BOOKS.
teach.b: Then he heard a sermon about Gandhi, and it moved him so much that he went out and bought books on Gandhi's life and work.
In them he saw love lifted into a force that could move a whole community, without hatred and without weapons. That's the first half of the puzzle. The second half is what he didn't do.
King stayed a Christian minister. He didn't become a Hindu. What crossed the ocean was ahimsa, not-harming, an old Hindu vow.
In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras it comes first among the yamas, the restraints, and Patanjali promises that near someone rooted in not-harming, hostility falls away.
Gandhi's satyagraha put that vow to work in the street, and a Baptist pastor took it up to live out his own faith. King lists the marks of this nonviolence. It resists; it isn't for cowards.
It tries to win the opponent's friendship, not to humiliate them. It aims at the wrong, not at the people caught in it. And it accepts suffering without hitting back.
Winning the opponent over: many teachers hear Patanjali's old promise in that line.
So the puzzle solves itself. A method can travel. The faith underneath it doesn't have to be traded in for it.
Both stayed themselves, and they met in one movement.

how: King's Stride Toward Freedom is often read beside Gandhi's own writings, as his account of how satyagraha was carried into the American civil rights movement.

o: a Hindu teacher and his Baptist student, who studied together
a Hindu's method and a pastor's faith, meeting in one movement
two rival plans for change that clashed over nonviolence

games.q: who gave what — tap the pairs.
p: sent King out to buy books
aims at the wrong, not the people

s: King set aside his Christian faith to follow Gandhi
he stayed a minister; he wrote that Christ gave the spirit and Gandhi the method.
King went to buy books on Gandhi after hearing a sermon about him
he tells the story himself in Stride Toward Freedom.
nonviolence, as King describes it, is a way to avoid conflict
in his list it resists; it just won't humiliate the opponent or hit back.

games.q: your building's landlord ignores the broken heat. a neighbor wants to post his home address online to shame him. by the ahimsa King took from Gandhi, what fits?
o: press hard and in public, aiming at the cold flats, not at humiliating him.
post it: shame is the only thing that moves people like him.
say nothing: non-harm means never pushing back.
games.why: King's nonviolence resists, but aims at the wrong, not the person, and hopes to win him over. the Yoga Sutras' promise: near non-harm, hostility falls away.

practice: Bring to mind someone you're at odds with right now. Hindu teachers say ahimsa covers thought and word as well as deed, so start with the thought. Breathe in slowly, and on the out-breath wish them, silently, no harm.
If you pray, add their name to your prayer. Stay with it for a few breaths, even if the wish feels stiff at first.

wordCard.voice: Gandhi and King: today, a pastor's faith and a Hindu's method, meeting in one movement without either giving way.

orig.note: Sanskrit satya, truth, and agraha, holding firm: the method that crossed the ocean.

carryVoice: Your line from Gandhi and King: ahimsa, non-harm that wins the opponent over. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Stride Toward Freedom, ch. 6, 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence' (doubts about love in social conflict; a sermon on Gandhi and the books bought after; Christ the spirit and motivation, Gandhi the method; the marks of nonviolent resistance)
sources.work: Martin Luther King Jr., Stride Toward Freedom (paraphrased)

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 2.30 (the yamas, beginning with ahimsa) and 2.35 (where not-harming is established, hostility is abandoned in its presence)
